item.title: OpenAI releases three AI‑generated breakthroughs with expert shepherds
item.description:
OpenAI releases three AI‑generated breakthroughs with expert shepherds

On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, and said it would use expert “shepherds” to decide how to share the findings.

🔍 Overview

  • All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in their fields.
  • OpenAI describes the work as extending previous efforts and breaking new ground.
  • The company is working with expert “shepherds” who determine the release strategy for each result.

🧩 Results and Release Strategies

Discipline Claim Release Strategy
Mathematics Purports to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions AI‑generated output released; researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result
Computer Science Claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis External group of researchers assembled to explain the result
Physics Explores the Standard Model, quantum chromodynamics and its relationship to Yang‑Mills theory (does not address the mass‑gap problem) Deferred to an external group of experts; no material released yet

⚙️ How the shepherd model works

  • Expert “shepherds” decide how best to share each breakthrough.
  • Each discipline receives a distinct release approach.
  • Mathematics: output released directly, leaving researchers to explain it.
  • Computer science: OpenAI will assemble an external group of researchers to explain the result.
  • Physics: OpenAI will defer to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.

💡 Why it matters

  • The mathematics result targets the Kakeya conjecture, a problem linked to a recent Fields Medal.
  • The computer‑science claim challenges the exponential time hypothesis, a hypothesis closely related to the P vs NP Millennium Prize problem.
  • The physics work touches on quantum chromodynamics and Yang‑Mills theory, central to the Standard Model and another Millennium Prize problem.
  • Experts described the findings as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”
  • Researchers expressed concern that only hand‑picked experts initially see the work, saying “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”
  • Many welcomed the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds previously released, but questioned the restriction of access to OpenAI‑chosen experts.
  • Some argued that public announcement should also make the work available for anyone to scrutinize.

📚 Community reactions

  • Brown University professor Brendan Hassett said the claim “looks well supported,” though he had not yet checked the Lean formalization.
  • Constantin Kogler (Institute for Advanced Study) said, “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” while questioning the hand‑picked expert restriction.
  • Andreas Karch (University of Texas at Austin) called the hand‑picking “a disaster.”

#OpenAI #AIresearch #Mathematics #ComputerScience #Physics

Source: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs

item.title: OpenAI shares three AI‑generated breakthroughs in math, CS, and physics
item.description:
OpenAI shares three AI‑generated breakthroughs in math, CS, and physics

🔍 Overview

  • Less than a month after releasing hundreds of manuscripts with claimed solutions to long‑standing mathematics questions, OpenAI announced three new major discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics.
  • The company introduced a new collaboration model that uses external experts called “shepherds” to guide the work in computer science and physics, while for the mathematics result the experts advised releasing the AI output for researchers to examine.
  • OpenAI says it is taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results and is publishing the AI‑generated materials on GitHub.

🧪 What was discovered

  • Mathematics – The model produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture for the Euclidean wave equation in every spatial dimension (≥ 2). The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing, and it also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range.
  • Computer Science – The model disproves the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The accompanying paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed‑width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space; the case of 3‑SAT refutes the hypothesis.
  • Physics – The output includes a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, covering Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.

👥 Shepherds & Verification

  • A working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the computer‑science proof.
  • For the physics result, David Gross will lead a group that includes Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov.
  • The verification of the computer‑science result will be guided by the same three experts (Impagliazzo, Paturi, and Williams).

📂 Release & Open Letter

  • The AI‑generated write‑ups and Lean formalizations for the mathematics and computer‑science results were released on GitHub today.
  • At the request of the verification group, all materials were made public immediately so others can examine them.
  • OpenAI issued an open letter asking the community to discuss three broader questions:
    1. Expectations for early access, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and use of unpublished material.
    2. How credit should recognize both new discoveries and the work of checking, fixing, simplifying, explaining, and extending them.
    3. Ways to support students and researchers as methods change while preserving the judgment needed to question results and develop new ideas.

⚖️ Community & Policy considerations

  • The AGMAI panel of math advisers warned against the practice of designating certain people to receive output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation, and biased selection.
  • The panel recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, include Lean‑formalized proofs, provide information on how problems were chosen, fund people working on understanding the results, and supply other supporting details.

#OpenAI #AIResearch #Mathematics #ComputerScience #Physics

Source: OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
